(CNN) -- Kate Meinhardt felt like a clown jammed into a Volkswagen bug when she lived in a 21-square-foot room aboard a circus train. Kate Meinhardt crammed her life into a 21-square-foot room while she lived aboard a circus train. Bungee cords crisscrossed her walls once a week to prevent an avalanche of items from raining down. A microwave, mini refrigerator, her laptop and baskets of personal items lined the dorm-like room. Showering, going to the bathroom and even doing laundry became racing contests on the train, Meinhardt said. The 13 people on board shared one shower, two toilets and one washer and dryer. "It's a pretty tough life living in such a small space," she said. The 23-year-old spent almost a year as an animal handler for Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus. While most iReporters haven't run off to join the circus, some have traded in their homes for smaller digs. One iReporter even opted for a floating lifestyle, where he could sail away at a moment's notice. iReport.com: Living in tight quarters . Living on a 25-foot boat was only supposed to be temporary, but Jim Smith loved it so much he stayed there for a year. "I have lived in a 25-foot sailboat, a 28-foot motor home, a 32-foot sailboat and now an 800 square-foot apartment," Smith said in his iReport. "I was happiest with the 25-foot sailboat." While docked in Panama City, Florida, Smith kept his expenses to a minimum. The marina slip rent was only $200 and electricity was included in the rent, he said. The boat did not have refrigeration so Smith kept his food inside an insulated ice box. For 79 cents at the discount grocery store, he could buy a 10-pound bag of ice that would last him several days, even during the summer. Air conditioning wasn't a luxury Smith had either, but fans and sea breezes kept him cool. "Sometimes the less you have, the more you like it," he said. The portable lifestyle also charmed a father-son duo who set out on a yearlong European vacation. A camper van took them wherever they wanted, whenever they wanted. Spencer Pearson and his 15-year-old son, Bryce, bought a 150-square-foot van in Germany for their European excursion. Living out of the van meant "no reservations, no packing and unpacking of suitcases, no strange beds," Pearson said. Modern amenities weren't amiss on the van, which included everything from the Internet and entertainment to a complete bath and kitchen, and there were occasional hotel stays and meals out that made the trip more pleasant. The simple life also enticed Deborah Greant and her husband to trade in their Calgary, Canada, home for an RV. Both she and her husband have neuromuscular problems and needed extra help taking care of their large home. Since moving into a 240-square-foot RV, they can manage the house themselves. "We didn't want to be owned by our things," Greant said. "We jettisoned pretty much everything except things from former generations." While two people living in an RV can be tight, imagine a family of six trying to do the same. Mounting living expenses and a job relocation prompted the Chervenkas to sell their home and move into a 32-foot RV. Two pets came along, too. The Chervenkas weren't forced to do this. Their goal was to become debt-free and save money for their children's college educations. When pilot Tim Chervenka got transferred to Charlotte, North Carolina, the family set up camp in a 32-foot RV. The temporary situation turned into a permanent one. The family said goodbye to paying a first and second mortgage and pricey utilities. They now pay only $500 a month, utilities included. "It's made such an adjustment in our personal life without the juggling," Cindy Chervenka said. "We have so much more family time. It's a good feeling." Cindy Chervenka has some advice for others thinking of a drastic downsizing: "Step out of your comfort zone and try it. We didn't plan on doing this full-time, but once we discovered it, we thought, 'hey we can do this forever!' Until you step out and try it, you'll think it's not doable."

outputs.L1:
(CNN) -- Kate Meinhardt likened herself to a circus clown squeezed into a Volkswagen Beetle during the time she spent living in a mere 21-square-foot room aboard a circus train. She managed to compress her entire life into this cramped space, stringing bungee cords across her walls each week to prevent her belongings from tumbling down in an avalanche. The dorm-like quarters housed a microwave, a mini refrigerator, her laptop, and baskets of personal effects.

Aboard the train, even the most basic daily activities—showering, using the bathroom, and doing laundry—became races against time, according to Meinhardt. The 13 passengers shared a single shower, two toilets, and one washer-dryer set. "It's a pretty tough life living in such a small space," she reflected.

The 23-year-old spent nearly a year working as an animal handler for Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus. While most iReporters haven't gone so far as to join the circus, many have nonetheless embraced smaller living spaces, forgoing their conventional homes. One iReporter even chose a life on the water, ready to set sail at a moment's notice.

*iReport.com: Living in tight quarters*

What began as a temporary arrangement aboard a 25-foot boat became a year-long adventure that Jim Smith grew to cherish. "I have lived in a 25-foot sailboat, a 28-foot motor home, a 32-foot sailboat, and now an 800-square-foot apartment," Smith wrote in his iReport. "I was happiest with the 25-foot sailboat."

Docked in Panama City, Florida, Smith managed to keep his expenses remarkably low. His marina slip rent came to just $200 a month, with electricity included. Lacking refrigeration on board, he stored his food in an insulated ice box, relying on a 10-pound bag of ice—purchased for just 79 cents at a discount grocery store—to last several days, even through the summer heat. Air conditioning was likewise a luxury he did without, though fans and sea breezes kept him comfortably cool. "Sometimes the less you have, the more you like it," he observed.

This appeal of a portable lifestyle also captivated a father-son duo who embarked on a year-long European adventure, traveling wherever their whims took them in a camper van. Spencer Pearson and his 15-year-old son, Bryce, purchased a 150-square-foot van in Germany to serve as their home base for the journey. Life on the road meant "no reservations, no packing and unpacking of suitcases, no strange beds," Pearson explained. Yet the van was hardly lacking in modern comforts, equipped with internet access, entertainment systems, and a full bath and kitchen—complemented by the occasional hotel stay or restaurant meal to enhance the experience.

This same appeal for simplicity led Deborah Greant and her husband to exchange their home in Calgary, Canada, for life in an RV. Both suffering from neuromuscular conditions, the couple had struggled to maintain their large house without assistance. Since downsizing to a 240-square-foot RV, however, they've found they can manage their household needs independently. "We didn't want to be owned by our things," Greant explained. "We jettisoned pretty much everything except items passed down from former generations."

If two people sharing an RV sounds cramped, consider a family of six attempting the same feat. Faced with escalating living expenses and a job relocation, the Chervenka family made the decision to sell their home and move into a 32-foot RV, bringing along their two pets in the process.

For the Chervenkas, this wasn't a matter of necessity but of choice—driven by a desire to become debt-free and build savings for their children's college educations. When pilot Tim Chervenka was transferred to Charlotte, North Carolina, the family settled into their 32-foot RV, initially viewing the arrangement as temporary. It has since become their permanent way of life.

Free from the burden of a first and second mortgage, along with costly utility bills, the family now spends just $500 a month, utilities included. "It's made such an adjustment in our personal life without the juggling," said Cindy Chervenka. "We have so much more family time. It's a good feeling."

For others contemplating a similarly dramatic downsizing, Cindy Chervenka offers this counsel: "Step out of your comfort zone and try it. We didn't plan on doing this full-time, but once we discovered it, we thought, 'Hey, we can do this forever!' Until you step out and try it, you'll think it's not doable."

# Life on the Move: Extreme Housing Choices That Redefine Home

For most people, home is a fixed address—a place with ample square footage, modern conveniences, and a sense of permanence. But for a growing number of adventurous individuals, home has become something far more fluid, mobile, and unconventional. Their stories reveal that comfort and happiness don't always require traditional living spaces.

## Life Aboard the Circus Train

Kate Meinhardt's living situation would make even the most committed minimalist pause. For nearly a year, she called a mere 21-square-foot room aboard a circus train her home, working as an animal handler for the legendary Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus. To put that space in perspective, it's smaller than many walk-in closets—yet Meinhardt made it work through sheer ingenuity and adaptability.

Living in such tight quarters demanded creative problem-solving on a daily basis. Bungee cords became essential tools, used to secure her belongings and prevent them from shifting or falling as the train rumbled down the tracks. Perhaps most challenging was sharing minimal facilities with 13 other people. What might seem like mundane daily tasks—showering and doing laundry—transformed into competitive races against roommates, as everyone vied for limited time and resources. This unusual living arrangement required Meinhardt to develop patience, flexibility, and a good sense of humor about her circumstances.

## Setting Sail for Simplicity

While Meinhardt found her unconventional home on rails, Jim Smith discovered his aboard the water. Smith made the deliberate choice to live on a 25-foot sailboat for an entire year, and looking back, he considers it not just a memorable experience but genuinely the happiest period of his housing history. This is a notable claim, especially considering that Smith later owned both a motor home and a larger apartment—yet neither living situation matched the contentment he found on his modest vessel.

Financially, Smith's sailboat lifestyle proved remarkably economical. He paid just $200 per month for marina rent, a fee that conveniently included electricity—a cost that would be difficult to match with conventional housing in most markets. To further simplify his lifestyle and cut expenses, Smith forwent a standard refrigerator altogether. Instead, he relied on a discount ice-box method to keep his food fresh, embracing a simpler, more traditional approach to food storage that reduced both his costs and his environmental footprint.

## A Broader Movement Toward Minimalism

Meinhardt and Smith are far from alone in their embrace of unconventional living. Their stories represent just two examples from a wider community of iReporters who have chosen to step away from traditional housing in favor of minimalist or mobile lifestyles. Among these adventurous souls is a father-son duo who spent an entire year traveling through Europe together in a camper van, trading the stability of a permanent residence for the freedom of the open road and the opportunity to explore an entire continent while creating lasting memories together.

These stories collectively challenge conventional wisdom about what constitutes a "proper" home. Whether it's a cramped room on a circus train, a sailboat rocking gently in a marina, or a camper van winding through European countryside, these individuals demonstrate that with creativity, adaptability, and a willingness to embrace simplicity, home can take remarkably different forms—and sometimes, the smallest or most unconventional spaces lead to the greatest sense of freedom and satisfaction.

Others in the iReport community have shared similar stories of downsizing into campers, converting vehicles into full-time residences that let them travel while maintaining a stable, if compact, home base.

These varied experiences—whether born of necessity like Meinhardt's circus employment or chosen deliberately like Smith's sailboat life—reveal a common thread: living in significantly reduced square footage, while undeniably challenging, often leads to unexpected benefits. counterfactuals.output:
# Living Small: Meet the People Who Chose Life in Under 200 Square Feet

*An iReport Special*

---

**When Maria Chen sold her three-bedroom house in Portland to move into a 28-foot sailboat, her mother cried. Not out of sadness, but confusion. "She kept asking, 'Where will you put your books?'" Chen laughs. "I told her: fewer books, more ocean."**

Chen is part of a growing subculture of Americans who have made the deliberate choice to live in radically small spaces — boats, RVs, converted vans, even retired circus train cars. Their reasons vary, but a common thread runs through their stories: a rejection of the idea that bigger is better.

---

### The Sailor

Chen, 34, a former marketing executive, now lives aboard *Wanderlust*, a boat with roughly 150 square feet of livable space, docked seasonally along the Pacific coast.

"You'd think the hardest part is the lack of space," she said. "Actually, the hardest part is the lack of *distraction*. When you're in 150 square feet, you can't hide from your own life. You have to deal with things."

She showers using two gallons of water. Her kitchen is the size of a closet. But she says she's never felt more free.

"I used to have a mortgage, a garage full of things I never used, and a low-grade anxiety I couldn't name," Chen said. "Now I have a boat, a fishing rod, and a really good book light."

---

### The Circus Kids, All Grown Up

Not far from Sarasota, Florida — long known as a wintering ground for traveling circuses — retired train car communities still exist, home to former performers and roustabouts who never left the rails behind, literally.

Tommy Ruiz, 61, spent 40 years performing high-wire acts before retiring into a converted 1948 Pullman car that once housed circus wardrobe.

"This car is 10 feet wide, and it's seen more of America than most people ever will," Ruiz said, gesturing to the faded gold lettering still visible beneath a fresh coat of paint. "I don't need a mansion. I lived out of a trunk for four decades. This is basically a palace to me."

Ruiz says the small space keeps him connected to a rhythm of life he never wants to lose. "The circus teaches you that home isn't a place. It's the people, and how little you actually need."

---

### The Family of Four in 320 Square Feet

Not everyone downsizing is single or retired. The Whitfield family — two parents, two kids under 10 — has lived in a converted school bus, nicknamed "The Biscuit," for three years.

"People ask if it's hard," said dad Aaron Whitfield. "It's hard the way anything worthwhile is hard. But my kids have seen 38 states. They know how to fix a generator. They know how to get along with each other because there's nowhere to storm off to."

His wife, Dana, homeschools their children at a fold-down table that doubles as a bed at night. "We had a house once," she said. "This feels more like a home."

---

### Why Now?

Housing analysts point to rising costs, environmental awareness, and a cultural shift — accelerated by social media — that has romanticized minimalist living. Tiny house communities have sprouted across the country, and "van life" hashtags rack up billions of views online.

But those actually living the lifestyle caution against the Instagram version.

"People see the sunset photos," Chen said. "They don't see me pumping out the bilge at 2 a.m. in the rain."

Still, she wouldn't trade it.

"Small space, big life," she said. "That's the whole secret."

---

*Have you downsized your living space in a dramatic way? Share your story and photos with CNN iReport.*

# Living Small: How iReporters Are Redefining Home

*CNN iReport*

Across the country, a growing number of Americans are trading square footage for simplicity. CNN iReporters have been sharing their journeys into tiny houses, converted vans, and radically decluttered apartments — and their stories reveal a movement that's as much about mindset as it is about square footage.

## From McMansion to 220 Square Feet

Denise Okafor, an iReporter from Asheville, North Carolina, sold her 2,400-square-foot house three years ago and now lives in a tiny home she helped build herself.

"I used to spend my weekends cleaning rooms I never even walked into," Okafor wrote in her submission, which included photos of her sunlit loft bed and fold-down desk. "Now my whole house takes ten minutes to clean, and I actually have time to live in it."

Okafor says the hardest part wasn't the build — it was the emotional purge beforehand. "You don't realize how much stuff is holding you hostage until you have to decide whether it fits in 220 square feet."

## Life on Four Wheels

For Marcus Tran, minimalism means having no fixed address at all. Tran converted a used Ford Transit into a mobile home two years ago and has since driven it through 38 states.

"People assume I'm running from something," Tran said in his iReport, which featured a walkthrough video of his compact kitchen and solar setup. "Really, I'm running toward something — flexibility, mostly. If I don't like my neighborhood, I have a new one by Friday."

Tran acknowledged the trade-offs: no permanent shower, limited storage, and constant vigilance about power and water. "It's not glamorous every day. Some mornings it's just me, a French press, and a parking lot. But I wouldn't trade it."

## Downsizing as a Family

Not all tiny-living converts are solo adventurers. The Whitfield family — parents Rachel and Tom, plus their two kids — submitted an iReport documenting their move from a four-bedroom suburban home into a 34-foot travel trailer.

"Everyone told us we were insane," Rachel Whitfield wrote. "Four people, one bathroom, bunk beds stacked like a submarine. But something happened after the first month — we started talking to each other again instead of retreating to separate rooms."

Tom Whitfield added a practical note: "We saved more money living small in one year than we did in five years of a traditional mortgage. That's not nothing."

## The Common Thread

What unites these iReporters isn't the size of their homes so much as the philosophy behind them. As Okafor put it: "Minimalism isn't about deprivation. It's about deciding what actually deserves space in your life — literally and figuratively."

# Living Small: Four Unconventional Homes on the Move

*iReport Special: Real people share why they traded traditional houses for life in motion*

Home is often thought of as a fixed address—four walls, a roof, a mailbox. But for a growing number of people, home is wherever they park, dock, or pitch it. iReport spoke with four individuals and families who've embraced radically different, downsized lifestyles, each carving out a sense of permanence in spaces that are anything but conventional.

## The Circus Performer: Home Is Where the Tent Is

For aerial artist Mara Delgado, "moving day" happens every few weeks. Traveling with a touring circus troupe, she's lived out of a converted trailer for six years, packing her entire life into roughly 80 square feet.

"People assume it's chaotic, but it's actually the opposite," Delgado says. "When your space is that small, you become ruthless about what you keep. Everything has a place because there's nowhere else for it to go."

Her trailer includes a fold-down bed, a rack for her aerial silks and costumes, and a small propane stove. The hardest adjustment wasn't the size—it was the isolation that can come with constant travel. "You build community fast in circus life, though. Your neighbors are your coworkers, your family, your support system. The trailer is small, but the world around it isn't."

## The Sailor: A Life Measured in Nautical Miles

Tom Whitfield has spent the last four years living aboard a 34-foot sailboat, drifting between coastal marinas and open water. A former office manager, Whitfield sold his house, most of his belongings, and bought *Wanderlust*, a boat he now calls the best decision he's ever made.

"You learn to live with the rhythm of the water instead of fighting it," he says. "There's no yard to mow, no roof to fix—well, there is, technically, but it's called a sail."

Storage is Whitfield's biggest daily challenge. Every item on board serves at least two purposes, and non-essentials are ruthlessly avoided. He relies on solar panels for power and fishes for part of his food. "The tradeoff is you give up a lot of convenience. What you get back is silence, stars, and total self-sufficiency."

## The Road-Tripping Family: Europe as a Living Room

The Larsen family—parents Erik and Ingrid, and their two children, ages 7 and 10—have spent the past year touring Europe in a converted van, treating the continent itself as their backyard.

"We wanted our kids' classroom to be the Alps, the Mediterranean coast, cobblestone streets in places most people only see in photos," Ingrid explains. Their van includes bunk beds, a compact kitchen, and a fold-out table where the kids do schoolwork between border crossings.

Logistics are a constant puzzle—finding campsites, navigating language barriers, homeschooling on the move—but the family says the payoff is worth it. "Our kids have learned more geography and history by simply being in these places than any textbook could teach them," Erik says.

## The RV Family: Full-Time Life on Four Wheels

For the Bennett family of five, downsizing from a 2,400-square-foot house to a 320-square-foot RV wasn't just about saving money—it was about reclaiming time together.

"We were all so busy in our old life. Work, school, activities—we passed each other in the hallway more than we actually talked," says mom Casey Bennett. Now, the family travels between national parks, taking on remote work and online schooling as they go.

Space is tight with three kids, and privacy is a luxury few RV families take for granted. But Casey says the trade-off has reshaped their relationships. "We argue about normal things—whose turn it is to do dishes, who left wet towels on the floor. But underneath it, there's this constant closeness we didn't have before."

---

**A Common Thread**

Despite their vastly different circumstances—circus performer, sailor, road-tripping family, RV dwellers—all four share a common philosophy: less space often means more freedom. Trading square footage for mobility, and material possessions for experience, has redefined what "home" means for each of them.

As Delgado puts it: "Home was never really about the walls. It's about what you build inside them—or, in my case, what you build even when there aren't any."

*Have an unconventional living story to share? Submit your iReport today.*

# The Big Move to Small Spaces: Why More Americans Are Downsizing to Vans, Boats, and Tiny Homes

**PORTLAND, Ore.** — Three years ago, Maya Chen was paying $1,800 a month for a one-bedroom apartment she rarely saw during daylight hours. Today, she pays nothing in rent, showers under waterfalls, and calls a converted 2019 Ford Transit her home.

"I used to think success meant more square footage," Chen said, sitting on the fold-out bed that doubles as her living room couch. "Now I measure it in freedom."

Chen is part of a growing movement of Americans trading traditional housing for life in vans, sailboats, and trailers — a shift that accelerated during the pandemic but shows no signs of slowing down. While exact numbers are hard to pin down, van conversion companies report waitlists stretching months, and social media hashtags like #vanlife and #boatlife have amassed billions of views collectively.

## The Push and the Pull

For many downsizers, the decision isn't purely aspirational — it's economic.

"Rent ate 60% of my paycheck," said Marcus Webb, a freelance graphic designer who sold most of his belongings in 2021 to live in a 32-foot sailboat docked in Marina del Rey, California. "I did the math. In five years, I'll have saved enough to actually buy property outright, instead of just handing money to a landlord forever."

Housing costs have climbed nationally, with median home prices surging over 40% since 2020 in many metro areas, according to housing market data. For younger generations facing student debt and stagnant wages, alternative living isn't just quirky — it's practical.

But affordability tells only part of the story. Therapists and researchers point to something deeper: a growing rejection of consumer culture itself.

"I kept buying things to fill an apartment I was never in because I was always working to pay for the apartment," said Dana Torres, who converted a vintage Airstream trailer into her full-time home in Arizona. "It was this endless loop. Getting rid of 90% of my possessions felt like exhaling for the first time in a decade."

## Life in Motion

The daily reality of micro-living requires serious adaptation. Water conservation becomes second nature. Bathroom logistics — composting toilets, public showers, marina facilities — demand constant planning. Weather dictates everything from mood to mobility.

Tom Alvarez, who has lived in a renovated school bus for six years with his wife and two dogs, said the learning curve was steep.

"Our first winter, our pipes froze solid in Utah and we had no water for four days," Alvarez recalled, laughing. "We ugly-cried in a Walmart parking lot. But you adapt. Now I know more about propane systems and solar panel angles than I ever thought I'd need to."

Despite hardships, many describe unexpected gifts: closer relationships, deeper presence, and a recalibrated relationship with material things.

"My daughter used to have a room stuffed with toys she ignored," said Rachel Kim, who now lives with her family in a converted shuttle bus touring national parks. "Now she has twelve toys she actually plays with, and she's outside constantly. I don't know how to explain what that's done for her — and for us."

## Not Without Sacrifice

The lifestyle isn't universally romantic. Isolation, limited privacy, and the logistics of work, healthcare, and mail delivery pose ongoing challenges. Some downsizers eventually return to conventional housing after burnout.

"People see the Instagram photos of sunsets and think it's a permanent vacation," Webb said. "Nobody posts the video of you elbow-deep in a broken water pump at 2 a.m."

Still, for those who've stuck with it, the trade-offs feel worthwhile.

"I don't own much anymore," Chen said, gesturing to her compact kitchen, "but somehow I feel like I have more than I ever did before."

As housing costs climb and questions about work, purpose, and consumption continue reshaping American life, the movement toward smaller living may be less a fringe trend and more a signal of larger cultural shifts — one converted van, boat, and trailer at a time.
